cases.rationale: Changed recovery behavior selects this policy and receives runtime failure and recovery checks. Its SSDF boundary limits framework claims even when the project verification passes.

cases.input: A library maintainer changes a public serialized response by adding an optional generation field. The report labels this offline contract evidence and doesn't claim semantic retrieval or live provider quality.
cases.boundary_evidence: Internal refactors with unchanged public behavior can reuse existing contract tests. Synthetic fixtures don't prove semantic retrieval or live provider quality.
cases.rationale: Changed public serialization selects this policy and receives consumer-boundary verification. Passing synthetic contract fixtures still doesn't establish semantic retrieval or live provider quality.

cases.input: An API producer adds an optional field; tests show old consumers ignore it and existing request/response meanings stay unchanged, so the supported API version stays the same.
cases.boundary_evidence: A proven compatible optional field can keep the current API version. SemVer doesn't prescribe HTTP path versioning or a universal deprecation duration.
cases.rationale: A proved compatible optional field doesn't require an incompatible API-version migration.

cases.input: An API keeps its documented safe error format; status handling and caller recovery tests pass without adopting RFC 9457 problem details.
cases.boundary_evidence: RFC 9457 is an optional common error format. Existing documented error formats can remain; this policy doesn't require converting every response into problem details.
cases.rationale: RFC 9457 is optional. Keeping another documented safe format doesn't itself violate the HTTP error contract.

cases.input: An API returns a fixed two-item in-memory enumeration, with no unbounded collection or tenant-sensitive cursor; it omits pagination.
cases.boundary_evidence: RFC 8288 defines links, not a mandatory pagination algorithm. Cursor format, limits, and consistency guarantees are project choices; fixed small in-memory results can omit pagination.
cases.rationale: The policy explicitly allows fixed small in-memory results to omit pagination; it doesn't mandate a cursor for every response.

cases.input: A database operator tests a migration and recovery on the selected engine and reports its measured recovery behavior without claiming the same DDL or numeric target for other engines.
cases.boundary_evidence: Database DDL and transaction behavior vary by engine. Online migration patterns and recovery time targets require a workload-specific decision; no universal numeric target is prescribed.
cases.rationale: Engine-specific proof doesn't establish universal DDL behavior or a universal recovery-time target.

cases.input: A service uses an outbox with separately tested duplicate handling and compensation; it doesn't claim a database rollback reverses an external payment.
cases.boundary_evidence: The PostgreSQL example doesn't establish identical guarantees for every datastore. Outboxes, compensation, and distributed transactions are design options that need their own proof.
cases.rationale: An outbox is an allowed design option when its own effect and recovery proof is supplied; a distributed transaction isn't universally required.

cases.input: A repeated background task replaces the same public cache entry with identical bytes; the harmless repeat and its workload scope are explicitly documented.
cases.boundary_evidence: Exactly-once delivery isn't inferred from a queue setting. Deduplication scope and retention are workload decisions; an explicitly harmless repeat can be documented as such.
cases.rationale: A documented harmless repeat doesn't require the same deduplication mechanism as a repeated financial charge.

cases.input: An optional integration stays explicitly disabled at startup and has no credential; it isn't activated or invoked while disabled.
cases.boundary_evidence: Optional integrations can remain disabled when their settings are absent. Validate their required settings before explicit activation; enabled features can't defer required security, correctness, or data-integrity checks beyond startup.
cases.rationale: Absent optional settings don't invalidate startup while the integration remains disabled. Required settings must be validated before activation.

cases.input: A service chooses its read deadline from measured dependency latency and the caller's budget; it doesn't copy an example percentile as a universal requirement.
cases.boundary_evidence: Timeout values follow measured latency, acceptable failure rates, and caller budgets. AWS example percentiles aren't universal requirements; non-idempotent effects need extra protection.
cases.rationale: The timeout follows the measured workload and caller budget. The cited article's example percentile isn't a mandatory global default.

cases.input: An operator reports separate expensive and cheap operation measurements and avoids certifying capacity from an aggregate request count.
cases.boundary_evidence: Per-customer quotas and degradation require product decisions. A request count alone doesn't certify capacity for unequal-cost operations; this policy supplies no universal throughput claim.
cases.rationale: Unequal-cost operations need workload evidence; a single requests-per-second count doesn't establish capacity.

cases.input: A handler stops collecting private request bodies and keeps only operation ID and failure class, instead of collecting bodies for a later redactor.
cases.boundary_evidence: Redaction is defense in depth; prefer not collecting sensitive values. Sampling, retention, and identifiers need workload and privacy review; structured JSON alone doesn't prove safe logging.
cases.rationale: Avoiding sensitive collection is preferred; the logging policy doesn't require recording a private value merely to redact it.

cases.input: A child operation creates a new span ID while retaining valid parent trace identity and safe correlation fields.
cases.boundary_evidence: Trace and span IDs have different roles. A new child span normally gets a new span ID; preserve valid trace identity without requiring every hop to repeat the same span ID.
cases.rationale: A child span normally gets a new span ID. Preserving trace identity doesn't require repeating the parent's span ID.

cases.input: A liveness probe reports that the process is responsive; a separate readiness probe rejects traffic when the required generation can't be read.
cases.boundary_evidence: Liveness, readiness, dependency diagnostics, and end-user success serve different purposes. Probe design and alert targets are project recommendations, not mandated by Google SRE.
cases.rationale: Liveness and readiness answer different questions. A dependency failure needn't make the liveness probe claim the process is dead.

cases.input: A release records exact patch pins and platform inputs but doesn't claim bit-for-bit reproducibility until independent rebuild evidence exists.
cases.boundary_evidence: Exact patch pins alone don't prove bit-for-bit reproducibility. Document platform, toolchain, network inputs, and remaining nondeterminism before making that claim.
cases.rationale: Exact versions alone don't prove bit-for-bit reproducibility; the narrower build record is valid without that unproved claim.

cases.input: A consumer verifies an artifact digest and trusted provenance identity but doesn't label the builder SLSA-certified or assess an entire SSDF program.
cases.boundary_evidence: SLSA levels depend on their full track requirements and trust model. This selected guidance doesn't assess a builder or certify SSDF, SLSA, or OSPS compliance.
cases.rationale: Selected artifact checks don't establish a complete framework level or certification; their narrower verified result can still be reported.
